input: The conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen into formaldehyde over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst has attracted considerable attention, and this study compares two different catalyst forms under identical test conditions. The performance of each catalyst is assessed primarily in terms of the space-time yield, defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), a metric that captures how productively the catalyst volume is being used. All of the tests were carried out at 250 °C and 50 bar, using a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and a single feed composition, in order to ensure a fair and consistent comparison. The structured catalyst delivered a space-time yield of 0.75 kg L-1 h-1, together with a remarkably low pressure drop of 0.29 bar and an activity loss of just 8% after 100 h on stream. By contrast, the conventional pellet catalyst achieved a space-time yield of only 0.46, with a substantially higher pressure drop of 1.5 bar and a more pronounced activity loss of 18% after 100 h. Taken together, these results clearly demonstrate the advantages of the structured form under the conditions investigated. It should be noted, however, that no sulfur-containing feed was tested, and it is also worth bearing in mind that space-time yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge, which can make comparisons of this kind difficult to find in the literature.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde. Two catalyst forms, structured and pellet, are compared on one feed, with space-time yield as the comparison measure: the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). The tests ran at 250 °C and 50 bar, at a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition. The structured catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.75 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.29 bar, and an activity loss of 8% after 100 h. The pellet catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.46, a pressure drop of 1.5 bar, and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h. The structured form leads on all three measures at the tested conditions: more product per unit catalyst volume, a smaller pressure drop across the charge, and a slower loss of activity over the test period. The comparison ranks the two charges as tested, at one temperature, one pressure, and one feed composition; it does not separate the effect of the form from the effect of the preparation, which the test design holds together. Pressure drop is a charge property as much as a catalyst property, and the gap between the forms is read with the charge geometry in view. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and behaviour on such a feed is unmeasured. Space-time yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, so the paired figures here give a comparison the literature usually lacks.
